cooling_items.text:
Cooling is provided by a central York water-cooled chiller located in the roof top main mechanical room. The chiller was manufactured in 2022 and is in good condition.Heat rejection is provided via a B.A.C. cooling tower installed in 2023. 

The condenser water system, including the cooling tower fan and condenser water pumps, are equipped with VFDs.

The chilled-water distribution system appears to be functioning normally, with supply and return piping, pumps, and control valves observed to be in serviceable condition at the time of the walkthrough. According to site staff, the chiller operates reliably under typical summer conditions.

Suite-level cooling is provided by in-suite fan coil units operating under local thermostatic control. These fan coils distribute chilled water from the central plant to provide space cooling throughout the suites. 

At the time of the site visit, the chiller and cooling tower were seasonally shut down, which is typical for the time of year. No major physical deficiencies were identified during the walkthrough, and building staff reported generally reliable operation during the most recent cooling season.
cooling_items.title: Fancoil + chiller

cooling_items.text:
Cooling control is currently provided through standalone controllers operates based on fixed setpoints and manual seasonal scheduling, with no centralized Building Automation System (BAS) integration observed.

Overall, the Cooling System appear to be in generally good condition at the time of the site visit. However, without BAS coordination, opportunities for optimized chiller staging, condenser water temperature reset, chilled-water temperature reset, and demand-based scheduling remain limited.

Future optimization could include BAS integration to enable centralized monitoring, automated seasonal changeover, temperature reset strategies, and improved fault detection. Such enhancements would improve system efficiency, reduce unnecessary runtime, and support long-term operational reliability.
cooling_items.title: Over all Good condition – No BAS Integration

dhw_items.title: Central DHW boilers plant

dhw_items.title: Atmospheric DHW Boiler

dhw_items.text: Two (2) indirect storage tank was observed, located at the main boiler room and is heated via DHW boiler. The tank was observed to be in good mechanical condition. storage temperature was observed at 150 F
dhw_items.title: Indirect storage tank

dhw_items.text: Thermostatic mixing valves set to approximately 120°F were observed and appeared to be in good mechanical condition.
dhw_items.title: Mechanical Mixing valves

dhw_items.text:
Domestic hot water complaints were reported in the West Tower during peak demand periods (approximately 8:00 AM and 6:00 PM), particularly in the mid and upper zones. Lower zone performance was reported to be stable during these periods.

Site review confirmed that DHW boiler capacity is adequate and that storage tank and mixing valve setpoints are operating within normal ranges. Based on these observations, the issue is not related to insufficient boiler capacity or control setpoints.

The temperature drop during peak demand may be associated with storage tank sizing relative to peak draw, zoning distribution imbalance, or recirculation performance in upper zones 

Further review of storage volume, recirculation flow rates, and zoning configuration is recommended to confirm root cause.
dhw_items.title: DHW balancing issue+ Future optimization BAS

Hot water generated by the boilers is distributed to in-suite fan coil units and also serves additional hydronic loads, including radiation, and heat exchanger circuits. heating_items.title: Good condition + Working normally

measures.existing_conditions: The existing HVAC mechanical systems—including MUAs, exhaust fans, heating boilers, DHW plant, cooling equipment, and pumps—are controlled manually or via basic local thermostats and temperature sensors. There is minimal outdoor-air reset, limited boiler sequencing, and no centralized scheduling or monitoring. Equipment often operates during unoccupied periods, leading to excessive energy use and chronic overheating.
measures.notes: Install a new central BAS to Control boilers, DHW, MUAs, pumps and exhaust fans with scheduling, reset and remote access, reducing energy use and maintenance. Improve building operation and management.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to install a centralized BAS to control all major HVAC systems. The BAS would provide occupancy-based scheduling, outdoor-temperature reset for boilers, zone-level temperature modulation, real-time monitoring, remote access, and alarm notifications. Improved control will reduce unnecessary run time, lower energy consumption, and improve comfort while reducing maintenance costs through better diagnostics. Utility incentives for advanced building controls can further improve project economics, with typical paybacks on the order of 3–4 years.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

measures.existing_conditions: The existing piping arrangement separates the WSHP loop, primary heating loop, and domestic hot water (DHW) loop into independent hydronic systems, each served by dedicated boilers and pumping configurations. The primary heating loop operates at higher temperatures for space heating, the WSHP loop operates at lower temperatures, and the DHW system functions on a separate loop without hydraulic or control integration. This configuration increases system complexity and limits opportunities for load diversity, heat recovery, and coordinated temperature optimization. During shoulder seasons, independent loop operation can contribute to boiler short cycling, elevated supply temperatures, and reduced overall plant efficiency.
measures.measure_title: Primary–Secondary Boiler and Hydronic Loop Reconfiguration (Primary loop + WSHP loop + DHW loop)
measures.notes: Reconfigure Primary heating loop, WSHP loop and DHW loop to a primary–secondary layout, hydraulically separating loops to improve temperature control, boiler protection and plant efficiency.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to evaluate reconfiguring the WSHP loop, primary heating loop, and DHW piping into a coordinated Primary–Secondary (P-S) hydronic arrangement. Under a P-S configuration, a central boiler primary loop would maintain controlled supply temperatures while secondary loops draw only the required flow and temperature for each load. This arrangement provides hydraulic separation, allows differentiated temperature control for high- and low-temperature systems, improves outdoor-air reset effectiveness, and reduces short cycling. Improved integration may also enhance return-water temperature control, supporting more efficient boiler operation. When implemented in conjunction with condensing boiler upgrades, this redesign may allow optimization of boiler staging and potential reduction in total boiler count, thereby lowering long-term maintenance complexity and operating costs. Further engineering review is required to confirm detailed hydraulic configuration, load diversity assumptions, and control sequencing strategy.
*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics.
Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

measures.existing_conditions:
Domestic hot water complaints were reported in the West Tower during peak demand periods (approximately 8:00 AM and 6:00 PM), particularly affecting the mid and upper zones. Lower zone performance was reported to remain stable during these periods.

Site review confirmed that DHW boiler capacity appears adequate, and both storage tank and mixing valve setpoints were observed to be operating within normal ranges. Based on these observations, the issue does not appear to be related to insufficient boiler capacity or improper control setpoints.

The temperature drop during peak demand may instead be associated with storage tank volume relative to peak demand, hydronic distribution imbalance between building zones, or insufficient DHW recirculation performance serving upper floors.
measures.measure_title: DHW Peak Demand Temperature Mitigation & Distribution Review
measures.notes: Investigate DHW temperature drop during peak demand periods through storage sizing review, recirculation analysis, and distribution balancing to identify corrective measures.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends conducting a targeted engineering investigation of the domestic hot water system to identify the root cause of peak demand temperature fluctuations.

This review may include evaluation of storage tank effective volume relative to peak draw profiles, verification of DHW recirculation flow rates, assessment of zoning distribution between lower, mid, and upper floors, and review of pump and balancing valve operation.

Where applicable, integration of temperature monitoring and recirculation control into a centralized Building Automation System (BAS) could improve system visibility, enable trend analysis during peak demand periods, and support long-term operational optimization.

measures.existing_conditions:
During the site walkthrough, the main fresh air intake serving the building ventilation system was observed to be located directly above the building’s garbage loading area. Building staff reported that during garbage collection periods, noticeable odours are occasionally drawn into the building through the ventilation system.

This condition may allow garbage odours or contaminants to enter the building through the make-up air intake during waste handling operations.
measures.measure_title: Garbage Odour Mitigation – Fresh Air Intake Relocation / Ducting Review
measures.notes: Review fresh air intake location above garbage loading area and evaluate intake relocation or duct modifications to mitigate odour entrainment.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends reviewing the ventilation intake configuration to reduce the potential for odour entrainment from the garbage loading area.

Potential mitigation strategies may include relocation of the fresh air intake, installation of duct extensions to relocate the intake to a cleaner air zone, or modification of the intake orientation and screening to improve separation from the loading area.

*Further engineering review is required to confirm the most appropriate solution while maintaining required ventilation airflow rates and code compliance.

measures.notes: Plan and install EV charging infrastructure for residents and staff, contact us for more detail.

Upgrading through the Trade‑In Program is recommended to replace outdated units with OCPP‑networked TAR‑M chargers, providing managed access, usage metering, and load balancing. *Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:

ventilation_items.text: Ventilation for the building is provided by One (1)make-up air (MUA) units, located in roof top, serving corridors and other public areas.
ventilation_items.title: Rooftop MUA

ventilation_items.text:
The building is equipped with one (1) central MUA unit located in the penthouse serving most residential floors, and three (3) fresh-air MUA units located in the ground-floor mechanical room serving common areas.

The penthouse central MUA is equipped with a VFD, during the site visit it was observed operating at approximately 48 Hz (80%). The ground-floor MUA units include two units with VFDs;

No occupancy-based scheduling or demand control was observed, three (3) fresh-air MUA units appear to operate at or near constant speed regardless of actual ventilation demand.

All units are equipped with heating and cooling coils served by glycol loops connected to the primary heating and cooling systems through shell-and-tube heat exchangers. These heat exchangers are difficult to service, limiting maintainability and increasing long-term operational risk.

The MUA systems were observed to be functionalwere originally installed circa 2004. Based on typical service life expectations for commercial ventilation equipment, the units are approaching the end of service life.
While no immediate deficiencies were identified, the current configuration presents opportunities for improved control, energy efficiency, and future lifecycle upgrades.
ventilation_items.title: 1 central MUA w\ VFD + 2 MUA w VFD + Plate and frame heat exchangers

ventilation_items.text: All units are equipped with heating and cooling coils served by glycol loops connected to the primary heating and cooling systems through plate and frame heat exchanger. These heat exchangers are in general good conditions.
ventilation_items.title: Plate and frame heat exchanger

ventilation_items.text:
Although the AHU units are in generally good mechanical condition, the building is not equipped with a centralized Building Automation System (BAS) to coordinate AHU operation with the rest of the mechanical systems.

Integration of the existing VFD-controlled AHU units into a BAS would enable improved scheduling, supply air temperature reset, demand-based ventilation, and alarm monitoring. These enhancements would improve overall energy performance, operational oversight, and long-term system reliability.
ventilation_items.title: AHU units with VFD capacity, but not integrate into BAS

ventilation_items.text: Supply-air temperatures and airflow patterns were generally consistent with normal operation. Hydronic heating coils are served from the building’s high-temperature heating loop. Overall, the MUA systems appear to be functioning as intended, with minor operational and control improvements possible to enhance performance and consistency.
ventilation_items.title: Hydronic MUA + good conditions

ventilation_items.text: Ventilation for the building is provided by One (1)make-up air (MUA) units, located in roof top, serving corridors and other public areas.
ventilation_items.title: Rooftop MUA

ventilation_items.text:
The building is equipped with one (1) central MUA unit located in the penthouse serving most residential floors, and three (3) fresh-air MUA units located in the ground-floor mechanical room serving common areas.

The penthouse central MUA is equipped with a VFD, during the site visit it was observed operating at approximately 48 Hz (80%). The ground-floor MUA units include two units with VFDs;

No occupancy-based scheduling or demand control was observed, three (3) fresh-air MUA units appear to operate at or near constant speed regardless of actual ventilation demand.

All units are equipped with heating and cooling coils served by glycol loops connected to the primary heating and cooling systems through shell-and-tube heat exchangers. These heat exchangers are difficult to service, limiting maintainability and increasing long-term operational risk.

The MUA systems were observed to be functionalwere originally installed circa 2004. Based on typical service life expectations for commercial ventilation equipment, the units are approaching the end of service life.
While no immediate deficiencies were identified, the current configuration presents opportunities for improved control, energy efficiency, and future lifecycle upgrades.
ventilation_items.title: 1 central MUA w\ VFD + 2 MUA w VFD + Plate and frame heat exchangers

ventilation_items.text: All units are equipped with heating and cooling coils served by glycol loops connected to the primary heating and cooling systems through plate and frame heat exchanger. These heat exchangers are in general good conditions.
ventilation_items.title: Plate and frame heat exchanger

ventilation_items.text:
Although the AHU units are in generally good mechanical condition, the building is not equipped with a centralized Building Automation System (BAS) to coordinate AHU operation with the rest of the mechanical systems.

Integration of the existing VFD-controlled AHU units into a BAS would enable improved scheduling, supply air temperature reset, demand-based ventilation, and alarm monitoring. These enhancements would improve overall energy performance, operational oversight, and long-term system reliability.
ventilation_items.title: AHU units with VFD capacity, but not integrate into BAS

ventilation_items.text: Supply-air temperatures and airflow patterns were generally consistent with normal operation. Hydronic heating coils are served from the building’s high-temperature heating loop. Overall, the MUA systems appear to be functioning as intended, with minor operational and control improvements possible to enhance performance and consistency.
ventilation_items.title: Hydronic MUA + good conditions
